name: Glossary of Tarot — the Golden Dawn's words
description:
# Glossary of Tarot

Short, sourced entries for the words the cards and courses lean on: the ten sephiroth, the twenty-two Hebrew letters, the signs, planets and elements, and the ideas (Book T, dignities, decans, Ma'at). Each entry is one paragraph with its sources. Rendered at [tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html); the deck and course texts link here by `scripts/link_glossary.py`. Entries are edited here, by hand.

sections.Entry:
A diagram of ten spheres, the [sephiroth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#sephirah), joined by twenty-two [paths](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#path). The Golden Dawn drew it after the Christian-Kabbalist tree of Athanasius Kircher (1652) and laid the whole tarot on it: each trump on a path, each Ace in Kether, each small card Two to Ten in the sephirah of its number ([Book T](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#book-t)). The Kabbalah it rests on was taken from a living Jewish tradition and refitted to a Victorian scheme; the [The Golden Dawn — the Map and the Walk](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=walking-the-golden-dawn-path) course says more. Not to be confused with this library's *Tree of Tarot*, a family tree of decks.

[See the map](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/tree-of-life.html)

sections.Entry: Hebrew for a numbered sphere, or emanation: the ten stations of the [Tree of Life](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#tree-of-life), from [Kether](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#kether) (1) to [Malkuth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#malkuth) (10). Mathers gives their names in English as Crown, Wisdom, Understanding, Mercy, Strength, Beauty, Victory, Splendour, Foundation and Kingdom. In [Book T](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#book-t) the small cards are "classified under the nine Sephiroth below Kether": the Twos in Chokmah, the Threes in Binah, and so on to the Tens in Malkuth.

sections.Entry:
The *Sepher Yetzirah* opens: "In two and thirty most occult and wonderful paths of wisdom". The ten [sephiroth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#sephirah) count as the first ten, and the twenty-two letters of the [Hebrew alphabet](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#hebrew-letters) as the rest. The Golden Dawn numbered the letter-paths 11 to 32 and gave each one a trump, so a trump is a way *between* two sephiroth rather than a place: Justice, path 22, runs from [Geburah](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#geburah) to [Tiphareth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#tiphareth).

[See the 22 paths on the map](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/tree-of-life.html)

sections.Entry: The twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, which the Golden Dawn set on the twenty-two [paths](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#path) in alphabetical order, Aleph on path 11 to Tau on path 32. The *Sepher Yetzirah* sorts them into three mothers (Aleph, Mem, Shin), seven doubles and twelve simple, or single, letters; the Order gave the mothers to the elements, the doubles to the seven planets and the simples to the twelve signs. Which planet goes with which double differs between versions of the *Sepher Yetzirah*; the Order made its own choice.

sections.Entry: The Golden Dawn's own paper on the tarot, set down mainly by S. L. MacGregor Mathers around 1888 and kept among initiates until Aleister Crowley printed it in *The Equinox* in 1912. It gives each card its title, its place on the [Tree of Life](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#tree-of-life) and in the zodiac, a description, a meaning, and a method of divination read by [dignities](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#dignities). It is a different text from Mathers's public booklet *The Tarot* (1888). Public domain; every card of this library's Golden Dawn deck carries its words.

sections.Entry: Book T's way of weighing a card in a spread: "A CARD is strong or weak, well dignified or ill dignified, according to the cards next to it on either side." Cards of the same suit strengthen it; Swords and Pentacles, Wands and Cups, weaken each other. Book T gives no rule for a card that lands upside down: the reversed meanings came later, through books printed for the public. The chapter [Dignities, not reversals](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=golden-dawn-dignities-not-reversals) sets the sources side by side.

sections.Entry: One of thirty-six ten-degree slices of the zodiac, three to a sign. [Book T](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#book-t) gives each decan to one small card, Two to Ten, and each a planetary ruler, beginning "from the royal Star of Leo": so the first decan, [Saturn](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#saturn) in [Leo](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#leo), is the Five of Wands. The card titles (Dominion, Ruin, Material Happiness) are read from these pairings.

sections.Entry: The Kabbalah's four levels of being, from the highest down: Atziluth (the Archetypal World), Briah (the Creative), Yetzirah (the Formative) and Assiah (the Material). This library's Golden Dawn deck sets the four suits in them, Wands in Atziluth, Cups in Briah, Swords in Yetzirah and Pentacles in Assiah, so the Two of Cups is Chokmah in Briah. Book T itself names Yetzirah, where the Aces rule "as the connecting link between Yetzirah and the Material Plane".

sections.Entry: A contemplative practice in which a trump is entered in imagination, as a way between two [sephiroth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#sephirah), rather than consulted for a meaning. The name belongs to the Order's heirs; the course [The Golden Dawn — the Map and the Walk](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=walking-the-golden-dawn-path) walks four of these gates. Pathworking, not prophecy: the card is a door you may choose to cross.

sections.Entry: The Egyptian idea of truth, balance and right order, and the goddess who stands for it, shown with an ostrich feather. In the judgment scene of the *Book of the Dead* the dead person's heart is weighed on a balance against the feather of Ma'at. Later readers set that balance beside the scales of the trump [Justice](https://tarot.recursive.eco/viewers/cards.html?src=../tarot/golden-dawn-book-t-tarot/grammar.json&item=major-11-justice); it is a comparison, not Book T's: Book T does not name her, and no tarot writer before Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs (1822), Court de Gébelin (1781) included, could have read her name.

sections.Entry:
**1. Kether**, the Crown. The first of the ten [sephiroth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#sephirah) of the [Tree of Life](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#tree-of-life), on the middle pillar. In [Book T](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#book-t) the four Aces stand here: they answer "to the Dominion of the Letters of the Name in the Kether of each".

Paths from here: [path 11](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/tree-of-life.html?path=11) (The Fool) to [Chokmah](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#chokmah); [path 12](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/tree-of-life.html?path=12) (The Magician) to [Binah](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#binah); [path 13](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/tree-of-life.html?path=13) (The High Priestess) to [Tiphareth](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/glossary.html#tiphareth).
